run.question:
Alertmanager alert RequestErrorRate (severity warning) is firing for service otel-demo/frontend-proxy since 2026-11-17T08:35:33Z.
Investigate why this alert is firing.

report.summary: The RequestErrorRate alert for otel-demo/frontend-proxy is backed by a real but very small error signal: frontend-proxy's server spans named 'ingress' carry status_code STATUS_CODE_ERROR continuously through the observed window (≈1.1–8.9 error spans per 5-minute step, 31.48 in the hour to 08:42:55) against ≈2,800–3,000 ingress spans per 5 minutes, i.e. an error ratio of about 0.0011, not the 0.0333 the alert annotation states. The exact mechanism is visible in the frontend-proxy access log: 10 responses '503 UC upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination}' between 08:27:01 and 08:39:15 (plus more in 08:20–08:25), i.e. Envoy's upstream connection to cluster 'frontend' was terminated before a response started, with fast durations (8–544 ms) and no HTTP status ever returned by the frontend. Nothing crashed: both the frontend pod frontend-675fd7b5c5-8qrfh and the frontend-proxy pod are Running/Ready with 0 restarts and empty lastState, no otel-demo events exist in the window, all flagd fault-injection flags in the flagd-config ConfigMap are 'off', and no other service shows request errors except low-rate flagd EventStream errors in ad, recommendation and fraud-detection. The deepest verified link is the frontend upstream terminating connections; why it does so (a keep-alive/idle-timeout reuse race is the best-fitting hypothesis) is not proven, because the frontend container emits no logs and its keep-alive settings are not visible in any readable object. The alert's '>0' threshold makes any residual error rate fire; a burst of three of these 503s at 08:35:09.864–08:35:10.114 immediately precedes the 08:35:33 alert start.

claims.text: frontend-proxy spans named 'ingress' with status_code STATUS_CODE_ERROR are present throughout the observed window: the 5-minute increase series moves between 0 and 8.89 error spans per step (e.g. 2.19 at 08:10:33, 8.89 at 08:24:33, 1.11 at 08:34:33, 6.67 at 08:36:33) while STATUS_CODE_UNSET ingress spans stay near 2,800–3,000 per 5 minutes; the hour ending 08:42:55 totals 31.48 ingress error spans versus 0 for the 'router frontend egress' client span.

The request error ratio computed from frontend-proxy's ingress spans at the alert's start instant 2026-11-17T08:35:33Z is 0.001131648 (increase over 5 minutes), i.e. roughly 30 times smaller than the 0.0333333 reported in the alert annotation.

The frontend-proxy container log of pod frontend-proxy-6b4d584985-p6mgt records 10 responses with exact text '503 UC upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination}' between 08:27:01.550Z and 08:39:15.955Z for paths /api/products/OLJCESPC7Z, /api/cart, /api/products/1YMWWN1N4O, /api/products/HQTGWGPNH4, /api/data/?contextKeys=travel, /api/products/66VCHSJNUP, /api/recommendations?productIds=0PUK6V6EV0 and /api/recommendations?productIds=HQTGWGPNH4, all against upstream cluster 'frontend', with request durations of 8–544 ms and no upstream response time recorded.

The same 503 UC upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination} signature also appears earlier in the window, e.g. 'GET /api/data/?contextKeys=assembly' at 08:20:54.654Z and 'GET /api/products/L9ECAV7KIM' at 08:21:10.280Z, and again at 08:37:12 and 08:37:45, so the error mechanism spans at least 08:20–08:39.

The failing requests are only a small minority of traffic: in the 08:35:00–08:35:02 slice of the frontend-proxy access log every logged response was 200 or 308 (34 requests), and the 503 UC lines are interleaved with continuous successful 200/308 traffic.

The frontend-proxy pod's own IP is 100.96.2.218 (pod frontend-proxy-6b4d584985-p6mgt) and the frontend pod frontend-675fd7b5c5-8qrfh has IP 100.96.2.139; therefore the 100.96.2.218:<port> fields in the 503 log lines are Envoy's local upstream/downstream socket addresses, and the log identifies the terminating upstream only by cluster name 'frontend'.

Among all services, only frontend-proxy (span 'ingress', 31.48 error spans/hour), fraud-detection ('flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream', 2.04), recommendation ('/flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream', 4.06) and ad ('flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream', 2.04) had a nonzero error-span increase in the hour ending 08:42:55; frontend, checkout, payment, cart and the other service spans had no nonzero error series in that query.

Pods frontend-675fd7b5c5-8qrfh and frontend-proxy-6b4d584985-p6mgt are both Running and Ready (all conditions True), with restartCount 0, empty lastState and container start time 2026-11-17T07:55:42Z; no OOMKilled or Evicted mark is present.

Cluster events in the window contain no event for any otel-demo object: all grouped events belong to namespace data-recorders (Job Completed/SuccessfulCreate, Pod Created/Scheduled/Started/Pulled/SuccessfulAttachVolume, PVC provisioning, one Pod FailedScheduling and one Killing, one PV VolumeFailedDelete).

The flagd-config ConfigMap's demo.flagd.json sets defaultVariant 'off' for every fault-injection flag, including paymentFailure, paymentUnreachable, cartFailure, adFailure, productCatalogFailure, recommendationCacheFailure, kafkaQueueProblems, emailMemoryLeak and imageSlowLoad.

The frontend container is CPU-limited to 100m (memory limit 200Mi) with no readiness or liveness probe; its CFS throttling ratio is 0.25–0.36 across the whole window (0.28 and 0.29 over the last 30 minutes), while frontend-proxy's container is throttled about 0.05.
The frontend container's memory working set grows slowly from 122.8 MB at 08:08:33 to 128.5 MB at 08:41:33 against a 200Mi limit, i.e. well below the limit and with no discontinuity.

frontend-proxy's client spans ('router frontend egress') show 0 error spans in the hour ending 08:42:55, so the frontend never returned a 4xx/5xx HTTP status to the proxy; the failures are connection-level terminations before any response, not application-level error responses from frontend.

A frontend pod crash, OOM kill, eviction or rollout is not what happened: both frontend and frontend-proxy pods are Ready with 0 restarts and empty lastState, the whole otel-demo set started 07:55:37–07:57:30 without subsequent events, and no otel-demo event appears in the event groups.

flagd fault injection as the source of these failures is not supported: every flag in the flagd-config ConfigMap is set to defaultVariant 'off', and no error spans appear on the services those flags would break (ad, cart, checkout, payment, product-catalog request spans show no errors in the hour); the only ad/recommendation/fraud-detection errors are on flagd EventStream gRPC spans at 2–4 per hour.

Best-fitting mechanism for the 503 UC failures: Envoy on frontend-proxy reused an idle HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection to the frontend (Next.js/Node) upstream that the frontend had already closed, so the connection was terminated before the response started. Supporting signs are the fast failure durations (8–544 ms, no upstream response time), the random spread across endpoints, and the burst of three failures within 250 ms at 08:35:09.864–08:35:10.114 that precedes the 08:35:33 alert. This is unverified: the frontend's keep-alive/idle-timeout settings are not in any readable ConfigMap and the frontend container produced no log lines.

Frontend CPU starvation may contribute to connection handling: the frontend container runs with a 100m CPU limit and 25–36% of its CFS periods are throttled for the whole window. This cannot by itself explain the timing of the alert, because the throttling ratio is steady before and during the alerting period and the failures occur in short bursts.

The alert annotation's current value 0.0333333 is not reproducible from the series available here and probably comes from an expression or metric not loaded in this Prometheus target (the target exposes only trace span metrics and resource metrics, and no alerting rules are loaded). It is therefore unsafe to read 0.0333 as a measured 3.3% request error rate.

Human follow-up: capture and retain frontend container logs (the frontend pod currently yields no log lines) to see the server side of these connection closes, and compare the frontend HTTP server keep-alive/idle timeout with Envoy's upstream idle timeout on the frontend route; adding a bounded retry policy on the frontend cluster would also convert most of these single-connection resets into successful retried requests.

Human follow-up: an alert whose condition is RequestErrorRate above 0 will fire on this persistent ~0.1% background reset rate; consider a small nonzero threshold, a minimum request volume, or a 'for' duration, and raise the frontend CPU limit (currently 100m with ~28% CFS throttling) as a capacity review item.

gaps: The alert rule definition is unavailable: list_prometheus_rules returned nothing for rule_name RequestErrorRate and nothing for all alerting rules, so the expression behind 'current: 0.0333333' cannot be read and that value could not be reproduced (observed 5-minute ingress error ratio at 08:35:33Z was 0.001131648).

The frontend container produced no log lines for 08:12:00–08:42:55 (fetch_pod_logs on frontend-675fd7b5c5-8qrfh returned 0 lines, 0 bytes), so the frontend side of the connection termination and any server-side keep-alive or timeout message could not be inspected.

No readable object holds the frontend's HTTP keep-alive/idle-timeout settings or the frontend-proxy Envoy upstream connection settings: only 4 ConfigMaps exist in otel-demo (flagd-config, kube-root-ca.crt, otel-collector, product-catalog-products) and the frontend-proxy container has no args and only environment variables.

Jaeger retained traces only through 08:08:24 (data_as_of 08:08:24–08:08:28), so no span of the 08:20–08:42 failure period could be inspected; tag searches for http.status_code 404/429/500/503/504 and for error=true / otel.status_code=ERROR / otel.status_code=Error in frontend-proxy returned nothing in that retained sample, so the per-error-span HTTP status/flag is not directly confirmed from traces (it is confirmed from the Envoy access log instead).

The frontend-proxy container log stream ends at 08:39:26, so the final ~3.5 minutes before the alert evaluation (08:39:26–08:42:55) could not be read; and the 4 MiB tail read covers only from about 08:20, so whether this 503 UC pattern already existed during 07:55–08:20 is unknown.

No pre-incident baseline exists for the error metric: frontend-proxy span-metric samples begin at 08:08:33 (30-minute aggregation source starts 08:12:55) although the pods started at 07:55:37, so it cannot be determined whether the ~0.1% reset rate is new or has been present since the environment was created.

The observed error-span counts (spanmetrics) do not match the log-sampled 503 counts exactly (e.g. 10 UC 503 lines in 12.25 minutes versus 6.67 error spans per 5 minutes at 08:38:33), so some ERROR-status spans may correspond to responses not captured in the log slices read; that share is unknown.
Whether the frontend's runtime flagd flag values differ from the ConfigMap defaults (all 'off') could not be verified, since flagd exposes no readable state or metric here.
The 'not_integrated' change_history source is unavailable, so no change record could be checked for the 08:35:33 alert start.
next_steps: Retrieve or enable frontend container logging (or frontend HTTP access logs) for 08:20–08:43 to observe the upstream server's connection close behaviour.

Inspect the frontend-proxy Envoy configuration (listener/route/cluster settings for the 'frontend' cluster: idle_timeout, max_requests_per_connection, retry_policy) and compare it with the frontend HTTP server's keep-alive/idle timeout; consider a retry policy on idempotent routes.
Review the frontend Deployment CPU limit (100m) against its sustained ~28% CFS throttling and memory growth from 122.8 MB to 128.5 MB, if capacity tuning is in scope.
Locate the platform-side rule that produces alertname RequestErrorRate, since it is not loaded in this Prometheus, and confirm its threshold and window against the measured ~0.1% ingress error ratio.
